introText: Twelve free-response problems spanning all four chapters (separable equations, linear equations and the integrating factor, second-order homogeneous equations, and nonhomogeneous equations solved by undetermined coefficients), Basic to Advanced. Try each one, then reveal the worked solution.

solution.en: \( dy=x^2\,dx \Rightarrow y=\dfrac{x^3}{3}+C \). \( y(1)=\dfrac13+C=2\Rightarrow C=\dfrac53 \). So \[ y=\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac53,\qquad y(2)=\frac83+\frac53=\frac{13}{3}. \]

question.en: Solve \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y}{x} \) for \( x,y>0 \), with \( y(1)=2 \). Find \( y(4) \).

solution.en: \( \dfrac{dy}{y}=\dfrac{dx}{x} \Rightarrow \ln y=\ln x+C \Rightarrow y=Ax \). \( y(1)=A=2 \), so \[ y=2x,\qquad y(4)=8. \]

\( \dfrac{dy}{y^2}=x\,dx \Rightarrow -\dfrac1y=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C \). \( y(0)=\tfrac12 \Rightarrow -2=C \). So \( -\dfrac1y=\dfrac{x^2}{2}-2 \Rightarrow y=\dfrac{-1}{\tfrac{x^2}{2}-2}=\dfrac{2}{4-x^2} \), and \[ y(1)=\frac{2}{3}. \] This solution's denominator vanishes at \( x=\pm2 \), so it's only valid on the interval \( -2<x<2 \) containing the initial point \( x=0 \) — it can't be extended past either pole.
\( \mu=e^{x} \): \( (e^{x}y)'=2e^{x} \Rightarrow e^{x}y=2e^{x}+C \Rightarrow y=2+Ce^{-x} \). \( y(0)=2+C=0\Rightarrow C=-2 \). So \[ y=2-2e^{-x},\qquad y(1)=2-2e^{-1}\approx1.264. \]

question.en: Solve \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{y}{x}=2 \) for \( x>0 \), \( y(1)=3 \). Find \( y(2) \).

solution.en: \( \mu=x \): \( (xy)'=2x \Rightarrow xy=x^2+C \Rightarrow y=x+\dfrac{C}{x} \). \( y(1)=1+C=3\Rightarrow C=2 \). So \[ y=x+\frac2x,\qquad y(2)=2+1=3. \]
\( \mu=e^{-x} \): \( (e^{-x}y)'=e^{-x}e^{2x}=e^{x} \Rightarrow e^{-x}y=e^{x}+C \Rightarrow y=e^{2x}+Ce^{x} \). \( y(0)=1+C=0\Rightarrow C=-1 \). So \[ y=e^{2x}-e^{x},\qquad y(1)=e^2-e. \]

question.en: Solve \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{2y}{x}=3x \) for \( x>0 \), \( y(1)=2 \). Find \( y(2) \).

solution.en: \( \mu=x^2 \): \( (x^2y)'=3x^3 \Rightarrow x^2y=\dfrac{3x^4}{4}+C \Rightarrow y=\dfrac{3x^2}{4}+\dfrac{C}{x^2} \). \( y(1)=\dfrac34+C=2\Rightarrow C=\dfrac54 \). So \[ y=\frac{3x^4+5}{4x^2},\qquad y(2)=\frac{53}{16}. \]

Auxiliary equation: \( r^2+4r+13=0\Rightarrow r=\dfrac{-4\pm\sqrt{16-52}}{2}=-2\pm3i \) — complex, with \( \alpha=-2 \), \( \beta=3 \), so \( y=e^{-2x}(C_1\cos3x+C_2\sin3x) \). \( y(0)=C_1=0 \), so \( y=C_2e^{-2x}\sin3x \); \( y'=C_2e^{-2x}(3\cos3x-2\sin3x) \), and \( y'(0)=3C_2=6\Rightarrow C_2=2 \). So \[ y=2e^{-2x}\sin3x,\qquad y(\pi/6)=2e^{-\pi/3}\sin(\pi/2)=2e^{-\pi/3}. \]

Homogeneous: \( r^2-4r+4=(r-2)^2=0\Rightarrow r=2 \) (repeated), so \( y_c=(C_1+C_2x)e^{2x} \). The forcing \( e^{2x} \) matches the repeated root, so the trial needs \( x^2 \): \( y_p=Ax^2e^{2x} \). Substituting gives \( 2Ae^{2x}=e^{2x} \) (the \( x \)- and \( x^2 \)-coefficients cancel automatically, as they must at a repeated root), so \( A=\tfrac12 \), \( y_p=\tfrac12x^2e^{2x} \). With \( y=(C_1+C_2x)e^{2x}+\tfrac12x^2e^{2x} \) and both conditions zero, \( C_1=C_2=0 \). So \[ y=\tfrac12x^2e^{2x},\qquad y(2)=2e^{4}. \]

Homogeneous: \( r^2+1=0\Rightarrow r=\pm i \), so \( y_c=C_1\cos x+C_2\sin x \). The forcing \( \sin x \) matches this pair exactly (resonance), so the trial needs an extra \( x \): \( y_p=x(A\cos x+B\sin x) \). Substituting and matching gives \( A=-2 \), \( B=0 \), so \( y_p=-2x\cos x \). With \( y=C_1\cos x+C_2\sin x-2x\cos x \): \( y(0)=C_1=0 \); \( y'=-C_1\sin x+C_2\cos x-2\cos x+2x\sin x \), \( y'(0)=C_2-2=1\Rightarrow C_2=3 \). So \[ y=3\sin x-2x\cos x,\qquad y(\pi)=0-2\pi(-1)=2\pi. \]
